column3: The earlier boat episode has the same pattern: Moses condemns an apparently harmful act whose protective purpose is later disclosed.
It directly explains the slain boy's anticipated burden on his believing parents, supplying the hidden future knowledge absent from Moses's judgment.
Allah's complete knowledge of the hidden and visible offers a broad theological counterpoint to Moses's knowledge limit.
The third episode again makes Moses assess an apparently puzzling act before its concealed benefit is explained, completing the narrative pattern.
It explains how damaging the boat protected its poor owners, a direct analogue for an apparently wrongful act serving a hidden mercy.
Its response to an unsettling, unrecognized encounter only loosely echoes Moses's shock at what he sees.
Moses recalls having killed a person and fears retaliation, giving a direct but differently framed connection to taking life.
It states the intended replacement of the slain boy with one more pure and tender, directly continuing the focus event.
Calling unfamiliar visitors unrecognized does not clarify the killing, innocence, or hidden knowledge in the focus.
The first murder condemns an unjust killing, providing a foundational ethical contrast to the focus's apparent killing.
This begins Moses's journey toward the encounter but adds no direct ethical or epistemic clarification of the killing.
The impotence of false gods has no substantive connection to the focus event.
The same rhetoric of condemning something as outrageous appears, but the accusation concerns Mary's childbirth rather than killing.
The journey's lost fish is only remote narrative setup for the focus.
Its prohibition on certainty about tomorrow reinforces the limit of human access to future outcomes central to the focus reading.
Moses's earlier killing and rescue create a direct narrative contrast with his later objection to the boy's killing.
Travel fatigue does not clarify the focus event.
The garden's undiminished produce is unrelated to the focus's moral and epistemic problem.
The announcement of a pure boy provides a close lexical and thematic counterpoint to the boy Moses calls pure.
The lost fish described as astonishing is only faintly parallel to the focus's startling event.
Voluntary remembrance does not materially illuminate the killing or its hidden rationale.
Its explicit prohibition on killing a soul except for a soul or corruption closely states the legal measure Moses invokes.
Returning along their tracks is narrative setup without direct bearing on the focus.
Allah's witness over everything broadly supports the hidden knowledge that qualifies Moses's visible judgment.
The shared travel verb has no thematic significance here.
Khidr's divinely granted mercy and special knowledge establish the authority and epistemic setting for the focus event.
It explicitly contrasts human claims with Allah's all-encompassing knowledge, supporting the focus's knowledge-limit theme.
Its severe punishment described as unrecognized shares language of enormity but not the focus's killing or hidden rationale.
Moses's request to learn from the specially taught servant directly frames the unequal knowledge exposed in the focus.
Divine wisdom and will provide only a broad theological backdrop to the exceptional event.
Individual awareness of what it has brought offers only a distant accountability parallel.
Khidr's warning that Moses cannot be patient with him directly anticipates Moses's reaction to the focus event.
The question about human creation does not clarify the focus.
Divine sole authority on the Last Day is too general to explain the focus's moral judgment.
Cosmic measure in creation has no close connection to the event.
It condemns the unjust killing of prophets and attaches punishment, supporting the moral gravity of wrongful killing.
Kinship precedence and divine knowledge are not relevant neighbours.
The fixed term of a soul's death provides only a general background for life and death.
The nearby observation that people are highly disputatious loosely frames Moses's repeated objections.
The cow's specification and slaughter do not illuminate the focus killing.
Allah's encompassing possession and knowledge are too general to be a close neighbour.
The demand for a sign is unrelated to the focus.
Producing a manifest sign has no material connection to the event.
Regret at final judgment does not clarify this narrative or its life-for-life measure.
Remembering Allah after forgetfulness and seeking nearer right guidance reinforces human dependence on divine guidance beyond present knowledge.
A promised knowledgeable boy in another narrative is not a substantive link.
Mocking signs and its punishment does not address the focus.
The imperative to proceed to punishment is unrelated.
Allah's effective creative command supplies only a very broad backdrop for divine action.
Its severe unrecognized punishment shares a term but concerns a rebellious town, not the focus killing.
Moses's pledge of patience and obedience immediately frames the promise broken by his objection in the focus.
The assurance that no soul is wronged supports the justice question raised by the apparent killing, though in final judgment context.
A marriage-work agreement does not bear on the focus.
Its commands of justice and protection of vulnerable property offer a broader ethical frame, but do not address killing directly.
Choosing to advance or delay has no close connection to the focus.
The birth of a forbearing boy is not a substantive neighbour.
It notes that divine willing exceeds human perception, but its subject is disbelief rather than the focus event.
Each soul being held for what it earned gives an accountability contrast to Moses's assessment of an apparently innocent soul.
The near formula of charging someone with an enormous matter parallels Moses's verbal condemnation, despite a different issue.
The mirage image of mistaken appearance loosely resonates with the focus's seen act and hidden reality.
Allah as creator and guardian is only a general theological background.
The miraculous promise of a son does not clarify the focus killing.
Denial of messengers is unrelated to the focus.
Transgression without right and ultimate return give a distant moral contrast to killing without apparent right.
The fate of earlier deniers offers only a broad sense of divine retribution.
The command to Moses to cast his staff is unrelated.
It rejects speaking about divine will without knowledge, a broad epistemic contrast to the focus's concealed divine purpose.
The promise of a knowledgeable boy is not a substantive connection.
Hearts rejecting the hereafter and their arrogance do not clarify the focus.
Its contrast between indecency and purity supplies moral vocabulary for the focus's pure soul, but not its exceptional rationale.
Unrecognized visitors do not illuminate the focus event.
Creation and provision are unrelated to the focus.
Following inherited custom does not clarify the killing or hidden future knowledge.
Created things running to fixed terms supply only a distant backdrop for divinely ordered outcomes.
The creation argument does not address the focus.
Prophetic teaching and purification offer only a broad association with the word purity.
Reviving the earth and the dead is not a close neighbour to the focus event.
It couples what is purer with Allah's knowledge where humans do not know, closely echoing the focus's purity and knowledge-limit themes in another setting.
Human desire for uprightness does not clarify the focus.
Commanding right and forbidding wrong is a broad moral frame, not a connection to the exceptional killing.
Sectarian mutual denial does not bear on the focus.
Moses is accused of intending to kill a soul as he did before and of acting tyrannically, directly echoing his concern in the focus.
Divine power not to coerce belief is only a distant distinction between divine capacity and human action.
Building the barrier does not clarify the focus's event.
Testing through loss of lives gives a broad suffering context but not the focus's moral or hidden-knowledge issue.
Regret over an evil companion is unrelated.
It distinguishes Allah's power from authority delegated to a messenger, a distant analogy to exceptional divinely informed action.
Recitation, guidance, and warning are not close neighbours.
The possibility of replacing humans with angels is unrelated to the slain boy's replacement.
The deathbed request to return supplies only a remote connection to death.
The brothers' fear of a wolf has no substantive link.
Allah's power and knowledge encompass everything, directly supporting the hidden-knowledge dimension at a general level.
The military test and trust in Allah do not clarify the focus.
Compensation for spouses lost to disbelievers is unrelated.
The garden companion's rebuke of disbelief does not illuminate the focus event.
Individual responsibility supports Moses's life-for-life reasoning only at a broad ethical level.
The breathing dawn is unrelated.
Allah's control over revelation is only a distant parallel to dependence on divinely granted knowledge.
Abraham's statement of illness is unrelated.
Comprehensive divine record-keeping broadly supports knowledge beyond the visible present.
It explicitly identifies the missing element in Moses's reaction: patience fails where one does not encompass the underlying knowledge.
Khidr's condition not to question an act before he explains it directly governs Moses's objection in the focus.
The first reminder after Moses's boat objection establishes the repeated pattern of reacting before the concealed rationale is given.
Moses's plea not to be blamed for forgetting records his response to the prior breach, but adds little to the killing itself.
The renewed, firmer reminder after the focus shows that the killing is the decisive second breach of the patience condition.
Moses accepts that another question will justify separation, completing the consequence of his focus-ayah objection.
Khidr's announced separation and promise to interpret the acts begins the explanation that reclassifies the apparent wrongdoing.
The wall's explanation supplies the third instance of hidden divine mercy behind an outwardly puzzling action, reinforcing the episode's interpretive rule.
The law of just retaliation states the life-for-life framework against which Moses judges the boy's killing.
It gives the preservation of life as the purpose of retaliation, sharpening the ethical force of Moses's objection.
A concealed killing is brought to light by Allah, linking taking life with knowledge not accessible to the disputing people.
Its censure of killing one's own people reinforces the gravity of unlawful killing, though in a communal covenant setting.
It condemns killing prophets without right, a direct instance of wrongful killing under divine judgment.
Its detailed rule for accidentally killing a believer marks the sanctity of life and the exceptional legal treatment of homicide.
It gives the grave consequence of deliberately killing a believer, strongly underscoring the moral presumption behind Moses's protest.
The Torah's life-for-life rule directly parallels the measure Moses invokes when he says the boy was not killed for another soul.
It expressly forbids killing the soul Allah has made sacred except by right, closely restating the focus's ethical objection.
It condemns the killing of children as an act made alluring by false partners, contrasting sharply with the focus's exceptional divinely informed act.
It calls killing children foolish and without knowledge, a pointed contrast to the focus's otherwise concealed knowledge-based rationale.
Its prohibition on killing children from fear of poverty affirms the child's inviolability against ordinary human calculations of future hardship.
It directly forbids killing the sacred soul except by right and regulates redress, making it one of the closest legal neighbours.
It lists killing a soul Allah has forbidden except by right among the gravest sins, closely supporting Moses's initial judgment.
Moses's accidental killing of a man and immediate remorse give important narrative background to his sensitivity about taking a life.
The buried girl being asked about her death presents an innocent child's killing as a matter requiring divine exposure and judgment.
Its question, 'for what sin was she killed,' directly foregrounds the injustice of killing an apparently blameless child.
